claim: Chromosome segregation during cell division requires engagement of kinetochores of sister chromatids with microtubules emanating from opposite poles.
source: Chromosome segregation during cell division requires engagement of kinetochores of sister chromatids with microtubules emanating from opposite poles.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about chromosome segregation.

claim: Bioriented sister kinetochores experience tension-dependent stabilization of microtubule attachments as the corresponding microtubules shorten.
source: As the corresponding microtubules shorten, these 'bioriented' sister kinetochores experience tension-dependent stabilization of microtubule attachments.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about kinetochore behavior.

claim: Stu2 is the yeast XMAP215 family member and microtubule polymerase.
source: The yeast XMAP215 family member and microtubule polymerase, Stu2, associates with kinetochores and contributes to tension-dependent stabilization in vitro.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Stu2 protein classification.

claim: Stu2 associates with kinetochores and contributes to tension-dependent stabilization in vitro.
source: The yeast XMAP215 family member and microtubule polymerase, Stu2, associates with kinetochores and contributes to tension-dependent stabilization in vitro.
evidence: This is a statement of prior experimental findings.

claim: A C-terminal segment of Stu2 binds the four-way junction of the Ndc80 complex.
source: We show here that a C-terminal segment of Stu2 binds the four-way junction of the Ndc80 complex (Ndc80c) and that residues conserved both in yeast Stu2 orthologs and in their metazoan counterparts make specific contacts with Ndc80 and Spc24.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Residues conserved both in yeast Stu2 orthologs and in their metazoan counterparts make specific contacts with Ndc80 and Spc24.
source: We show here that a C-terminal segment of Stu2 binds the four-way junction of the Ndc80 complex (Ndc80c) and that residues conserved both in yeast Stu2 orthologs and in their metazoan counterparts make specific contacts with Ndc80 and Spc24.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural data and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Mutations that perturb the Stu2-Ndc80c interaction prevent association of Stu2 with kinetochores.
source: Mutations that perturb this interaction prevent association of Stu2 with kinetochores, impair cell viability, produce biorientation defects, and delay cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations that perturb the Stu2-Ndc80c interaction impair cell viability.
source: Mutations that perturb this interaction prevent association of Stu2 with kinetochores, impair cell viability, produce biorientation defects, and delay cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mutations that perturb the Stu2-Ndc80c interaction produce biorientation defects.
source: Mutations that perturb this interaction prevent association of Stu2 with kinetochores, impair cell viability, produce biorientation defects, and delay cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Mutations that perturb the Stu2-Ndc80c interaction delay cell cycle progression.
source: Mutations that perturb this interaction prevent association of Stu2 with kinetochores, impair cell viability, produce biorientation defects, and delay cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ectopic tethering of mutant Stu2 species to the Ndc80c junction restores wild-type function in vivo.
source: Ectopic tethering of the mutant Stu2 species to the Ndc80c junction restores wild-type function in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3G-H and 4D-E.

claim: The role of Stu2 in tension-sensing depends on its association with kinetochores by binding with Ndc80c.
source: These findings show that the role of Stu2 in tension-sensing depends on its association with kinetochores by binding with Ndc80c.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bioriented attachment of sister chromatids to opposite poles of the mitotic spindle ensures accurate segregation of sister chromatids when a cell enters anaphase.
source: 'Bioriented attachment' of sister chromatids to opposite poles of the mitotic spindle in turn ensures that when a cell enters anaphase, each pair of sister chromatids segregates accurately (reviewed in Cheeseman, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: When correctly bioriented, a pair of cohesin-linked sister chromatids will be under tension from forces exerted by the shortening of opposing microtubules transmitted through the kinetochores.
source: When correctly bioriented, a pair of cohesin-linked sister chromatids will be under tension, from forces exerted by the shortening of opposing microtubules and transmitted through the kinetochores that connect spindle microtubules to chromosome centromeres.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about kinetochore mechanics.

claim: Tension-sensing and correction of erroneous attachments are critical mediators of genome integrity.
source: 'Tension-sensing' and correction of erroneous attachments are thus critical mediators of genome integrity.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the importance of tension-sensing.

claim: The Aurora B kinase (Ipl1 in budding yeast) is the immediate agent of error correction.
source: The Aurora B kinase (Ipl1 in budding yeast) is the immediate agent of error correction (Biggins and Murray, 2001; Biggins et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002; DeLuca et al., 2006; Hauf et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the absence of tension, Ipl1 phosphorylates Ndc80.
source: In the absence of tension, Ipl1 phosphorylates Ndc80 (DeLuca et al., 2006; Hauf et al., 2003), an essential part of the microtubule-contacting apparatus of a yeast kinetochore, and several other kinetochore substrates, including critical targets within the Dam1 complex (Biggins et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002; Kang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation by Ipl1 induces dissociation of a kinetochore from its associated microtubule.
source: Phosphorylation induces dissociation of a kinetochore from its associated microtubule, interrupting the incorrect attachment and allowing the attachment search to 'try again'.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the mechanism of error correction.

claim: Ndc80 is part of a rod-like assembly, the Ndc80 complex, a heterotetramer composed of two coiled-coil heterodimers, joined end-to-end in parallel orientations.
source: Ndc80 is part of a rod-like assembly, the Ndc80 complex, a heterotetramer composed of two coiled-coil heterodimers, joined end-to-end in parallel orientations (Alushin et al., 2010; Ciferri et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2005; Wilson-Kubalek et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The globular domain at the N-terminal end of Ndc80:Nuf2 contacts microtubules.
source: The globular domain at the N-terminal end of Ndc80:Nuf2 contacts microtubules; the globular domain at the C-terminal end of Spc24:Spc25 interacts, through two distinct adaptors, with the chromatin-proximal inner kinetochore.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural and functional knowledge.

claim: The globular domain at the C-terminal end of Spc24:Spc25 interacts, through two distinct adaptors, with the chromatin-proximal inner kinetochore.
source: The globular domain at the N-terminal end of Ndc80:Nuf2 contacts microtubules; the globular domain at the C-terminal end of Spc24:Spc25 interacts, through two distinct adaptors, with the chromatin-proximal inner kinetochore.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural and functional knowledge.

claim: The Ipl1 substrate residues of Ndc80 are in an N-terminal extension that contributes to the microtubule interface.
source: The Ipl1 substrate residues of Ndc80 are in an N-terminal extension that contributes, along with a globular, calponin homology domain, to the microtubule interface (DeLuca et al., 2006; Umbreit et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stu2 is the yeast ortholog of XMAP215/ch-TOG in metazoans.
source: A further component of the response to erroneous attachment is the plus-end microtubule polymerase, Stu2 (the yeast ortholog of XMAP215/ch-TOG in metazoans).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about protein orthology.

claim: Stu2's polymerization activity depends on plus-end binding through a set of N-terminal TOG domains.
source: Its polymerization activity depends on plus-end binding, through a set of N-terminal TOG domains (Figure 1A; Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Ayaz et al., 2012; Ayaz et al., 2014; Fox et al., 2014), but its kinetochore association is independent of microtubules (Hsu and Toda, 2011; Kakui et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019; Vasileva et al., 2017; Herman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stu2's kinetochore association is independent of microtubules.
source: Its polymerization activity depends on plus-end binding, through a set of N-terminal TOG domains (Figure 1A; Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Ayaz et al., 2012; Ayaz et al., 2014; Fox et al., 2014), but its kinetochore association is independent of microtubules (Hsu and Toda, 2011; Kakui et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019; Vasileva et al., 2017; Herman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In single-molecule experiments in vitro, kinetochores under low tension detach more frequently from microtubules than under higher tension, but only when Stu2 is present.
source: In single-molecule experiments in vitro, kinetochores under low tension detach more frequently from microtubules than under higher tension (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), but only when Stu2 is present (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: Cells lacking Stu2 have error-correction defects, including detached kinetochores, loss of biorientation, and spindle-assembly checkpoint-dependent cell cycle delay.
source: Cells lacking Stu2 have error-correction defects, including detached kinetochores, loss of biorientation, and spindle-assembly checkpoint-dependent cell cycle delay, although previous work has been unable to separate these phenotypes from pleiotropic effects arising from loss of Stu2 microtubule polymerase activity (Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Humphrey et al., 2018; Kosco et al., 2001; Miller et al., 2016; Pearson et al., 2003; Severin et al., 2001; Wang and Huffaker, 1997).
evidence: This is a statement of prior experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: Previous work has been unable to separate error-correction phenotypes from pleiotropic effects arising from loss of Stu2 microtubule polymerase activity.
source: Cells lacking Stu2 have error-correction defects, including detached kinetochores, loss of biorientation, and spindle-assembly checkpoint-dependent cell cycle delay, although previous work has been unable to separate these phenotypes from pleiotropic effects arising from loss of Stu2 microtubule polymerase activity (Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Humphrey et al., 2018; Kosco et al., 2001; Miller et al., 2016; Pearson et al., 2003; Severin et al., 2001; Wang and Huffaker, 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior work supported by citations.

claim: Stu2 associates with Ndc80c.
source: Stu2 associates with Ndc80c (Miller et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of prior experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: Recombinant full-length Stu2 binds directly to immobilized recombinant full-length Ndc80c.
source: Initial pulldown experiments showed that recombinant full-length Stu2 bound directly to immobilized recombinant full-length Ndc80c (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stu2 binds Ndc80cdwarf as efficiently as it does full-length Ndc80c.
source: In pulldown experiments, we found that Stu2 binds Ndc80cdwarf as efficiently as it does full-length Ndc80c (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A segment at the C-terminus of Stu2 (the CTS) is required for binding Ndc80c.
source: We found that a segment at the C-terminus of Stu2, most of which is conserved among budding and fission yeast and referred to here as the 'CTS' (Figure 1A), is required for binding Ndc80c.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Deletion of residues 857–867 of Stu2 results in loss of in vitro binding to Ndc80c.
source: Deletion of either an N-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 857–867), a C-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 868–888), or the stretch following the CTS that lacks conservation (residues 880–888) resulted in loss of in vitro binding (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Deletion of residues 868–888 of Stu2 results in loss of in vitro binding to Ndc80c.
source: Deletion of either an N-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 857–867), a C-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 868–888), or the stretch following the CTS that lacks conservation (residues 880–888) resulted in loss of in vitro binding (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Deletion of residues 880–888 of Stu2 results in loss of in vitro binding to Ndc80c.
source: Deletion of either an N-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 857–867), a C-terminal portion of the CTS (residues 868–888), or the stretch following the CTS that lacks conservation (residues 880–888) resulted in loss of in vitro binding (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The CTS binds dwarf Ndc80c with a dissociation constant of approximately 48 µM.
source: Fluorescence polarization binding experiments showed that the CTS binds dwarf Ndc80c with a dissociation constant of approximately 48 µM (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The C-terminal 33 residues of Stu2 are sufficient for Ndc80c binding.
source: Together, these data show that the C-terminal 33 residues of Stu2 are sufficient for Ndc80c binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The structure of the Ndc80cdwarf-Stu2 peptide complex was determined by molecular replacement.
source: We co-crystallized the Ndc80cdwarf with a 33-mer Stu2 peptide (Stu2 residues 855–888) and determined the structure of the complex by molecular replacement using the published Ndc80cdwarf structure as a search model (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the structural determination method.

claim: Clearly defined density in the electron density map corresponded to Stu2 residues 862–888.
source: Clearly defined density in the resulting map corresponded to residues 862–888; there was no density corresponding to the N-terminal seven residues (Figure 2B), and the C-terminal residues, 881–888, were part of a crystal-packing contact with the Nuf2 globular head of an Ndc80c symmetry mate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no density corresponding to the N-terminal seven residues of the Stu2 peptide.
source: Clearly defined density in the resulting map corresponded to residues 862–888; there was no density corresponding to the N-terminal seven residues (Figure 2B), and the C-terminal residues, 881–888, were part of a crystal-packing contact with the Nuf2 globular head of an Ndc80c symmetry mate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-terminal residues 881–888 of the Stu2 peptide were part of a crystal-packing contact with the Nuf2 globular head of an Ndc80c symmetry mate.
source: Clearly defined density in the resulting map corresponded to residues 862–888; there was no density corresponding to the N-terminal seven residues (Figure 2B), and the C-terminal residues, 881–888, were part of a crystal-packing contact with the Nuf2 globular head of an Ndc80c symmetry mate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A strong anomalous difference peak confirmed the correct sequence register of the Stu2 peptide model.
source: To resolve a potential ambiguity in the sequence register of the model, we determined the structure of a complex with a peptide containing selenomethionine in place of the methionine at position 876. A strong anomalous difference peak confirmed that we had chosen the register correctly (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Stu2 peptide binds at the junction of the two heterodimeric subcomplexes of Ndc80c.
source: The peptide binds at the junction of the two heterodimeric subcomplexes, contributing a fifth α helix, and packs at about 30° to the main axis of the four overlapping helices from Ndc80, Nuf2, Spc24, and Spc25.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Stu2 peptide contributes a fifth α helix to the Ndc80c junction.
source: The peptide binds at the junction of the two heterodimeric subcomplexes, contributing a fifth α helix, and packs at about 30° to the main axis of the four overlapping helices from Ndc80, Nuf2, Spc24, and Spc25.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Stu2 peptide packs at about 30° to the main axis of the four overlapping helices from Ndc80, Nuf2, Spc24, and Spc25.
source: The peptide binds at the junction of the two heterodimeric subcomplexes, contributing a fifth α helix, and packs at about 30° to the main axis of the four overlapping helices from Ndc80, Nuf2, Spc24, and Spc25.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Four conserved hydrophobic-residue side chains in the Stu2 CTS (V865, L869, I873, and M876) fit into hydrophobic pockets lined by conserved residues of Ndc80 and Spc24.
source: Four conserved hydrophobic-residue side chains in the Stu2 CTS (V865, L869, I873, and M876) fit into hydrophobic pockets lined by conserved residues of Ndc80 and Spc24 (Figure 2A–F), and in a conserved polar contact, the side chain of Stu2 R872 inserts between D651 and S654 on Ndc80 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The side chain of Stu2 R872 inserts between D651 and S654 on Ndc80 in a conserved polar contact.
source: Four conserved hydrophobic-residue side chains in the Stu2 CTS (V865, L869, I873, and M876) fit into hydrophobic pockets lined by conserved residues of Ndc80 and Spc24 (Figure 2A–F), and in a conserved polar contact, the side chain of Stu2 R872 inserts between D651 and S654 on Ndc80 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Immobilized Ndc80cdwarf did not bind any mutant version of the Stu2 C-terminus with L869A, I873A, or M876A mutations.
source: For the binding experiments we mutated L869, I873, and M876 to alanine. The immobilized Ndc80cdwarf did not bind any mutant version of the Stu2 C-terminus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The details of interaction between Stu2 and Ndc80c in the crystal lattice occur in solution as well.
source: These experiments show that the details of interaction between Stu2 and Ndc80c in the crystal lattice occur in solution as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pulldown experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Kinetochore co-immunoprecipitations from STU2-AID cells harboring stu2L869E,I873E,M876E (stu2EEE) mutations showed loss of Stu2-kinetochore binding.
source: Kinetochore co-immunoprecipitations from STU2-AID cells harboring either hydrophobic-to-charged or alanine mutations of these residues, stu2L869E,I873E,M876E (stu2EEE) or stu2L869A,I873A,M876A (stu2AAA), showed loss of Stu2-kinetochore binding (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Kinetochore co-immunoprecipitations from STU2-AID cells harboring stu2L869A,I873A,M876A (stu2AAA) mutations showed loss of Stu2-kinetochore binding.
source: Kinetochore co-immunoprecipitations from STU2-AID cells harboring either hydrophobic-to-charged or alanine mutations of these residues, stu2L869E,I873E,M876E (stu2EEE) or stu2L869A,I873A,M876A (stu2AAA), showed loss of Stu2-kinetochore binding (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The stu2EEE mutant showed a dramatic loss in kinetochore proximal signal compared to STU2WT.
source: We examined STU2-AID cells arrested in metaphase (using a CDC20-AID allele) that carried either STU2WT- or stu2EEE-GFP fusion variants. Compared to STU2WT, the stu2EEE mutant showed a dramatic loss in kinetochore proximal signal (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while displaying similar metaphase spindle length (measured by distance between Spc110-mCherry foci; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The stu2EEE mutant displayed similar metaphase spindle length to STU2WT.
source: We examined STU2-AID cells arrested in metaphase (using a CDC20-AID allele) that carried either STU2WT- or stu2EEE-GFP fusion variants. Compared to STU2WT, the stu2EEE mutant showed a dramatic loss in kinetochore proximal signal (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while displaying similar metaphase spindle length (measured by distance between Spc110-mCherry foci; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hydrophobic-to-charged or alanine mutations in the CTS of Stu2 resulted in a severe cell viability defect in the presence of auxin.
source: These same hydrophobic-to-charged or alanine mutations also resulted in a severe cell viability defect in the presence of auxin, exacerbated by addition of low concentrations of the microtubule destabilizing drug benomyl (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The cell viability defect of stu2 CTS mutations is exacerbated by addition of low concentrations of benomyl.
source: These same hydrophobic-to-charged or alanine mutations also resulted in a severe cell viability defect in the presence of auxin, exacerbated by addition of low concentrations of the microtubule destabilizing drug benomyl (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The individual stu2 mutations all had reduced cell viability.
source: The individual stu2 mutations also all had reduced cell viability (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 supplements 3-5.

claim: The hydrophobic residues in the CTS of Stu2, which contact Ndc80c in the crystal structure, are required for Stu2-kinetochore binding and cell viability in vivo.
source: Thus, the hydrophobic residues in the CTS of Stu2, which contact Ndc80c in the crystal structure, are required for Stu2-kinetochore binding and cell viability in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB were deficient for Stu2-kinetochore binding.
source: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB were deficient for Stu2-kinetochore binding as expected. Expressing NUF2-FKBP12 and adding rapamycin in culture rescued both the Stu2 binding defect (Figure 3G) and the cell viability defect of stu2EEE (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Expressing NUF2-FKBP12 and adding rapamycin in culture rescued the Stu2 binding defect of stu2EEE.
source: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB were deficient for Stu2-kinetochore binding as expected. Expressing NUF2-FKBP12 and adding rapamycin in culture rescued both the Stu2 binding defect (Figure 3G) and the cell viability defect of stu2EEE (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Expressing NUF2-FKBP12 and adding rapamycin in culture rescued the cell viability defect of stu2EEE.
source: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB were deficient for Stu2-kinetochore binding as expected. Expressing NUF2-FKBP12 and adding rapamycin in culture rescued both the Stu2 binding defect (Figure 3G) and the cell viability defect of stu2EEE (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Loss of kinetochore localization is the cause of viability loss in stu2EEE mutants.
source: Because rapamycin addition rescued both defects, we infer that loss of kinetochore localization is the cause of viability loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: stu2EEE is a true separation of function mutation that allows assessment of the cellular consequences of disrupting Stu2-kinetochore association.
source: Thus, stu2EEE is a true separation of function mutation that allows us to assess the cellular consequences of disrupting Stu2-kinetochore association.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The frequency of biorientation in STU2WT cells was 44 ± 2%.
source: The frequency of biorientation in STU2WT cells was at the level usually found in this assay (44 ± 2%, Figure 4A,B), but it was significantly lower in stu2EEE cells (16 ± 1%, p=0.0002).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The frequency of biorientation in stu2EEE cells was significantly lower (16 ± 1%, p=0.0002) than in STU2WT cells.
source: The frequency of biorientation in STU2WT cells was at the level usually found in this assay (44 ± 2%, Figure 4A,B), but it was significantly lower in stu2EEE cells (16 ± 1%, p=0.0002).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Most non-bioriented sister centromeres were found proximal to one of the two spindle poles in both STU2WT and stu2EEE cells.
source: We found that most non-bioriented sister centromeres were found proximal to one of the two spindle poles in both STU2WT and stu2EEE cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that biorientation defects are caused by the persistence of monopolar/syntelic attachments and not by lack of microtubule pulling forces.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 supplement 5.

claim: Biorientation defects in stu2EEE cells are caused by the persistence of monopolar/syntelic attachments and not by lack of microtubule pulling forces.
source: We found that most non-bioriented sister centromeres were found proximal to one of the two spindle poles in both STU2WT and stu2EEE cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that biorientation defects are caused by the persistence of monopolar/syntelic attachments and not by lack of microtubule pulling forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4 supplement 5.

claim: Cells defective in error correction depend on the spindle checkpoint to prevent chromosome missegregation and have a delayed metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Cells defective in error correction depend on the spindle checkpoint to prevent chromosome missegregation and have a delayed metaphase-anaphase transition (Biggins and Murray, 2001; Shonn et al., 2003; Stern and Murray, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There is a significant synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with deletion of MAD2 in the presence of low concentrations of benomyl.
source: We indeed found a significant synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with deletion of either of the spindle checkpoint components MAD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6) or MAD3 in the presence of low concentrations of benomyl (Figure 4C), likely due to severe aneuploidy in stu2EEE mad2Δ and stu2EEE mad3Δ cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 supplement 6.

claim: There is a significant synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with deletion of MAD3 in the presence of low concentrations of benomyl.
source: We indeed found a significant synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with deletion of either of the spindle checkpoint components MAD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6) or MAD3 in the presence of low concentrations of benomyl (Figure 4C), likely due to severe aneuploidy in stu2EEE mad2Δ and stu2EEE mad3Δ cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with mad2Δ or mad3Δ is likely due to severe aneuploidy.
source: We indeed found a significant synthetic growth defect of stu2EEE with deletion of either of the spindle checkpoint components MAD2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6) or MAD3 in the presence of low concentrations of benomyl (Figure 4C), likely due to severe aneuploidy in stu2EEE mad2Δ and stu2EEE mad3Δ cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the observed phenotype.

claim: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had greatly delayed anaphase onset.
source: Consistent with error correction defects, cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had greatly delayed anaphase onset, rescued by tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to the kinetochore with NUF2-FKBP12 and rapamycin (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to the kinetochore with NUF2-FKBP12 and rapamycin rescued the delayed anaphase onset of stu2EEE-FRB cells.
source: Consistent with error correction defects, cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had greatly delayed anaphase onset, rescued by tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to the kinetochore with NUF2-FKBP12 and rapamycin (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had marked errors in segregating chromosome III (18 ± 2%).
source: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had marked errors in segregating chromosome III (18 ± 2%, Figure 4E), which were nearly always rescued by tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to Nuf2-FKBP12 (4 ± 0.6%, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to Nuf2-FKBP12 nearly always rescued chromosome segregation errors (4 ± 0.6%).
source: Cells expressing stu2EEE-FRB had marked errors in segregating chromosome III (18 ± 2%, Figure 4E), which were nearly always rescued by tethering Stu2EEE-FRB to Nuf2-FKBP12 (4 ± 0.6%, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Correction of erroneous kinetochore-microtubule attachments in mitosis depends on kinetochore-bound Stu2.
source: We conclude that correction of erroneous kinetochore-microtubule attachments in mitosis depends on kinetochore-bound Stu2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rescue of the stu2EEE defect by ectopic tethering shows that CTS binding has a replaceable localization function.
source: Moreover, rescue of the defect by ectopic tethering shows that CTS binding has a replaceable localization function and that the effector function for error correction lies elsewhere in the Stu2 molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The effector function for error correction lies elsewhere in the Stu2 molecule (not in the CTS).
source: Moreover, rescue of the defect by ectopic tethering shows that CTS binding has a replaceable localization function and that the effector function for error correction lies elsewhere in the Stu2 molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: Previous studies have shown that Stu2 associates with kinetochores during mitosis in yeast cells.
source: Previous studies have shown that Stu2, a microtubule plus-end polymerase, associates with kinetochores during mitosis in yeast cells (He et al., 2001; Hsu and Toda, 2011; Kakui et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019; Vasileva et al., 2017) and contributes to the response to tension of kinetochores in vitro (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior findings supported by citations.

claim: Stu2 contributes to the response to tension of kinetochores in vitro.
source: Previous studies have shown that Stu2, a microtubule plus-end polymerase, associates with kinetochores during mitosis in yeast cells (He et al., 2001; Hsu and Toda, 2011; Kakui et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019; Vasileva et al., 2017) and contributes to the response to tension of kinetochores in vitro (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior findings supported by a citation.

claim: Kinetochore-bound Stu2 contributes to error correction in response to the absence of tension in vivo.
source: The findings reported here indicate that kinetochore-bound Stu2 indeed contributes to error correction in response to the absence of tension in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to diminished viability.
source: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to diminished viability, aberrant chromosome biorientation, synthetic growth defects when combined with a spindle checkpoint mutant, and anaphase onset delays – all phenotypes consistent with defects in error correction.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to aberrant chromosome biorientation.
source: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to diminished viability, aberrant chromosome biorientation, synthetic growth defects when combined with a spindle checkpoint mutant, and anaphase onset delays – all phenotypes consistent with defects in error correction.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to synthetic growth defects when combined with a spindle checkpoint mutant.
source: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to diminished viability, aberrant chromosome biorientation, synthetic growth defects when combined with a spindle checkpoint mutant, and anaphase onset delays – all phenotypes consistent with defects in error correction.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to anaphase onset delays.
source: Disrupting the Stu2:Ndc80c interaction led to diminished viability, aberrant chromosome biorientation, synthetic growth defects when combined with a spindle checkpoint mutant, and anaphase onset delays – all phenotypes consistent with defects in error correction.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chemically induced tethering of the mutant Stu2 to Ndc80c rescued all the defects examined, including viability and cell cycle progression delays.
source: Chemically induced tethering of the mutant Stu2 to Ndc80c rescued all the defects we examined, including viability and cell cycle progression delays.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The contributions of Stu2 to error correction in vivo depend on Ndc80c binding, not simply on its presence as a soluble factor or on its function as a microtubule polymerase.
source: Thus, the contributions of Stu2 to error correction in vivo depend on Ndc80c binding, not simply on its presence as a soluble factor or on its function as a microtubule polymerase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The required kinetochore localization of Stu2 might couple its polymerase activity specifically with growth and shrinkage at the plus-ends of kinetochore microtubules during metaphase.
source: Our results do not rule out, however, that the required kinetochore localization of Stu2 couples its polymerase activity specifically with growth and shrinkage at the plus-ends of kinetochore microtubules during metaphase.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Stu2's polymerase activity might be essential.
source: Its polymerase activity might therefore also be essential.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the previous statement.

claim: Stu2 association with Bik1 and Spc72 presumably couples its polymerase activity with other stages of spindle assembly or with other roles for microtubules in a yeast cell.
source: Stu2 association with Bik1 and Spc72 presumably couple this activity with other stages of spindle assembly or with other roles for microtubules in a yeast cell.
evidence: This is a speculation about the function of other Stu2 interactions.

claim: A published study of Stu2 dynamics at kinetochores using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching showed relatively high turnover.
source: A published study of Stu2 dynamics at kinetochores using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching showed relatively high turnover, and its authors suggested that Stu2 might not be a stably associated kinetochore factor (Aravamudhan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of prior findings supported by a citation.

claim: The bi-lobed clusters of Stu2 in metaphase cells probably contain both kinetochore-bound and purely microtubule tip-associated Stu2 pools.
source: The bi-lobed clusters of Stu2 in metaphase cells (Goshima and Yanagida, 2000; He et al., 2001; Pearson et al., 2001) probably contain both kinetochore-bound and purely microtubule tip-associated Stu2 pools, however, making definitive interpretation difficult.
evidence: This is a speculation about the composition of Stu2 clusters.

claim: Association of Stu2 with Ndc80c at the tetramer junction is necessary for its error correction function.
source: Our current data show that regardless of its exchange rate, association of Stu2 with Ndc80c at the tetramer junction is necessary for its error correction function and that tethering Stu2 to the junction is sufficient to restore full activity of an association-defective mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Tethering Stu2 to the Ndc80c junction is sufficient to restore full activity of an association-defective mutant.
source: Our current data show that regardless of its exchange rate, association of Stu2 with Ndc80c at the tetramer junction is necessary for its error correction function and that tethering Stu2 to the junction is sufficient to restore full activity of an association-defective mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Conservation of the four-component organization of Ndc80c from yeast to mammals suggests a conserved role for the connection between the two heterodimers.
source: Conservation of the four-component organization of Ndc80c from yeast to mammals, despite no evidence for independent functions of either heterodimer, suggests a conserved role for the connection between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary conservation.

claim: Several conserved features of the Ndc80c junction structure, including exposed hydrophobic pockets and a skipped α-helical turn near the N-terminus of Spc24, hinted that it might be a binding site for a conserved regulatory factor.
source: Several conserved features of the junction structure those crystals yielded, including exposed hydrophobic pockets and a skipped α-helical turn near the N-terminus of Spc24, indeed hinted that it might be a binding site for a conserved regulatory factor (Valverde et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior observations supported by a citation.

claim: Stu2 is at least one conserved regulatory factor that binds the Ndc80c junction.
source: Stu2 is evidently at least one such factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional findings.

claim: The Stu2 CTS adds a fifth helix to the four-helix bundle without producing any conformational rearrangements.
source: As now shown here, the Stu2 CTS adds a fifth helix to the four-helix bundle, without producing any conformational rearrangements, indicating that the role of the junction is simply to anchor Stu2 along the Ndc80c rod, rather than to receive an allosteric signal from it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: The role of the Ndc80c junction is simply to anchor Stu2 along the Ndc80c rod, rather than to receive an allosteric signal from it.
source: As now shown here, the Stu2 CTS adds a fifth helix to the four-helix bundle, without producing any conformational rearrangements, indicating that the role of the junction is simply to anchor Stu2 along the Ndc80c rod, rather than to receive an allosteric signal from it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: The structural findings do not rule out conformational switching by interactions between other parts of Stu2 and other parts of the Ndc80c.
source: That result does not rule out conformational switching by interactions between other parts of Stu2 thus anchored and other parts of the Ndc80c.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: Bulky hydrophobic residues are present at key positions in the CTS of Stu2 orthologs from fungi to metazoans.
source: Bulky hydrophobic residues are present at key positions in the CTS of Stu2 orthologs from fungi to metazoans, and the entire CTS sequence has conserved features (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The entire CTS sequence has conserved features.
source: Bulky hydrophobic residues are present at key positions in the CTS of Stu2 orthologs from fungi to metazoans, and the entire CTS sequence has conserved features (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The conservation of CTS features suggests that Stu2 orthologs also bind Ndc80c.
source: This conservation suggests that the orthologs also bind Ndc80c.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation.

claim: Published work provides evidence for interaction of the S. pombe Stu2 ortholog with the Ndc80 internal loop.
source: Published work provides evidence for interaction of the S. pombe ortholog with the Ndc80 internal loop (Hsu and Toda, 2011; Kakui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of prior findings supported by citations.

claim: The C-terminal position of the Ndc80c attachment segment of Stu2 and the length of the flexible linker would allow more distal parts of the protein to interact with almost any other site along the Ndc80c rod.
source: The C-terminal position of the Ndc80c attachment segment of Stu2 and the length of the presumably flexible linker between it and the dimerizing coiled-coil would allow more distal parts of the protein to interact with almost any other site along the Ndc80c rod, including the Ndc80 internal loop and the globular head (Miller et al., 2019), and probably even allow the TOG domains to contact the curled plus-ends of an attached microtubule.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: Additional interactions between Stu2 and Ndc80c are likely to be critical contributors to the mechanism by which Stu2 responds to tension or its absence and synergizes with the error-correcting detachment activity of Ipl1.
source: These additional interactions are likely to be critical contributors to the mechanism by which Stu2 responds to tension or its absence and synergizes with the error-correcting detachment activity of Ipl1.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional importance of additional interactions.
